content: Sea-buckthorn, scientifically known as Hippophae L., belongs to the family Elaeagnaceae and is a deciduous shrub. The name sea-buckthorn is hyphenated to distinguish it from the unrelated buckthorns of the genus Rhamnus in the family Rhamnaceae. It is also referred to as sea buckthorn, seabuckthorn, sandthorn, or seaberry. The plant is recognized by various names in different languages, such as Shaji in Chinese, Duindoorn in Dutch, Tyrni in Finnish, Argousier in French, Sanddorn in German, Olivello Spinoso in Italian, Облепиха (Oblepicha) in Russian, Espino de Mar or Espino Amarillo in Spanish, and Havtorn in Swedish and Danish. Since 2005, sea-buckthorn berries have gained significant attention in the global functional food industry, particularly in developed countries, due to their exceptional nutrient profile, antioxidant properties, and potential as a superfruit. Description and Distribution Sea-buckthorn comprises six species and twelve subspecies, native to a vast region spanning Europe and Asia, including countries such as China, Mongolia, India, Nepal, Pakistan, Russia, Great Britain, France, Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, Poland, Finland, Sweden, and Norway. Approximately 90% of the global sea-buckthorn resources, covering about 1.5 million hectares, are found in China, where the plant is extensively used for soil and water conservation. The shrubs typically grow to heights of 0.5–6 meters, though they can occasionally reach up to 18 meters in Central Asia. They thrive in dry, sandy environments, are tolerant of saline air and soil, and require full sunlight for optimal growth. They do not tolerate shade from larger trees. The most widespread species, Hippophae rhamnoides (common sea-buckthorn), has a range extending from the Atlantic coasts of Europe to northwestern China. In Western Europe, it is primarily found along sea coasts, where salt spray prevents competition from larger plants. In Central Asia, it is more common in arid, semi-desert regions, while in Central Europe and Asia, it can also be found as a subalpine shrub above the tree line in mountainous areas or along sunny riverbanks. The common sea-buckthorn has dense, stiff, and thorny branches. The plant is dioecious, meaning male and female flowers are borne on separate plants. Male plants produce brownish flowers that release wind-dispersed pollen. Berries and Leaves Female sea-buckthorn plants produce orange berries that are 6–9 mm in diameter, soft, juicy, and exceptionally rich in vitamin C, with concentrations averaging 600 mg per 100 g and sometimes reaching up to 1500 mg per 100 g. Some varieties are also abundant in vitamin A, vitamin E, and oils. These berries serve as an essential winter food source for certain bird species, such as fieldfares. The leaves are consumed by the larvae of various Lepidoptera species, including the coastal race of the Ash Pug moth, Brown-tail, The Dun-bar, Emperor Moth, Mottled Umber, and Coleophora elaeagnisella. The species Hippophae salicifolia (willow-leaved sea-buckthorn) is native to the Himalayas, growing at high altitudes in dry valleys south of the range of H. rhamnoides. It is characterized by broader (up to 10 mm wide), greener (less silvery) leaves and yellow berries. Another species, Hippophae tibetana (Tibetan sea-buckthorn), is found at even higher altitudes in the alpine zone. It is a low-growing shrub, typically not exceeding 1 meter in height, with small leaves measuring 1–3 cm in length. Two additional species, Hippophae goniocarpa and Hippophae neurocarpa, have been described in China, though their status as distinct species is not widely accepted. Harvesting and Landscaping Harvesting sea-buckthorn berries is challenging due to the dense thorns on the shrubs. A common method involves cutting entire branches, which are then frozen to facilitate berry removal. However, this approach is destructive to the plant and reduces future yields. The branches are frozen to −32°C, slightly defrosted during berry removal, and then cleaned. The berries are crushed to remove up to 95% of leaves and debris, which causes slight melting of the berries' surface. The cleaned berries are stored at −22°C. A more efficient harvesting method involves using a berry-shaker, a device developed in Estonia, which minimizes damage to the branches. However, mechanical harvesting leaves up to 50% of the berries in the field and can only be performed biennially, yielding about 25% of the potential harvest. During the Cold War, Russian and East German horticulturists developed new sea-buckthorn varieties with improved nutritional value, larger berries, varied ripening times, and branch structures that facilitate easier harvesting. In the past two decades, experimental sea-buckthorn crops have been cultivated in the United States (Nevada and Arizona) and in western Canada. The plant is also popular in landscaping, particularly as a vandal-proof barrier hedge due to its aggressive basal shoot system. It is used in some regions to stabilize riverbanks and steep slopes. In northern climates, sea-buckthorn is valued for its ornamental qualities, as its colorful berry clusters persist through winter. Florists also use its branches for decorative purposes. The plant is the regional flora of Satakunta, Finland. Nutrients, Potential Health Effects, and Cosmetics Sea-buckthorn berries are highly nutritious but very acidic and astringent, making them unpleasant to consume raw unless they are bletted (softened by frost) or mixed with sweeter substances like apple or grape juice. They are used in various products, including jams, juices, pies, and liquors. When pressed for juice, the berries separate into three layers: a thick orange cream on top, a middle layer rich in unsaturated fats, and a sediment-juice layer at the bottom. The top two layers are processed for cosmetic products like skin creams and liniments, while the bottom layer is used for edible products like juices and jams. Sea-buckthorn berries are rich in antioxidants, which may have potential benefits in reducing inflammation, preventing cancer, and managing other diseases. The fruit contains high levels of vitamin C, ranging from 114 to 1550 mg per 100 g, with an average of 695 mg per 100 g—approximately 12 times the vitamin C content of oranges. The berries also contain carotenoids, vitamin E, amino acids, dietary minerals, β-sitosterol, and polyphenolic acids. The oils derived from the seeds and pulp have been studied for their nutritional properties and are used in cosmetics and nutritional supplements. The juice has a freezing point of −22°C, allowing it to remain liquid in sub-zero temperatures. India's Defence Research Development Organization has utilized sea-buckthorn juice to create a multi-vitamin herbal beverage for troops stationed in extremely cold environments, such as Siachen. Traditional Medicine Sea-buckthorn has been used in traditional medicine for centuries, particularly in Asia, to treat various ailments. In China, it is used to relieve coughs, aid digestion, improve blood circulation, and alleviate pain. In Mongolia, extracts from the branches and leaves are used to treat gastrointestinal issues in both humans and animals. The bark and leaves are used to manage diarrhea, gastrointestinal and dermatological disorders, and rheumatoid arthritis. The flowers are used as skin softeners. In Indian, Chinese, and Tibetan medicine, the berries are incorporated into treatments for pulmonary, gastrointestinal, cardiac, blood, and metabolic disorders due to their hemostatic and anti-inflammatory properties. The berries and their derivatives are also used for colds, fever, exhaustion, stomach ulcers, cancer, and metabolic disorders. The oil, known as Chharma in some native languages, is used for liver diseases, inflammation, gastrointestinal disorders, eczema, canker sores, wounds, burns, frostbite, psoriasis, lupus erythematosus, and chronic dermatoses. In ophthalmology, berry extracts have been used to treat keratitis, trachoma, eyelid injuries, and conjunctivitis. Organizations The International Center for Research and Training on Seabuckthorn (ICRTS) was established in 1988 through a collaboration between the China Research and Training Center on Seabuckthorn, the Seabuckthorn Office of the Yellow River Water Commission, and the Shaanxi Seabuckthorn Development Office. ICRTS published the research journal Hippophae from 1995 to 2000, though it is no longer active. In 2005, the European Commission funded an international collaboration called EAN-Seabuck, involving the European Union, China, Russia, and other states, to promote sustainable crop and product development from sea-buckthorn.
